coverage players standing 25 yards downfield would be past the spot they are trying to reach. Under every version
of the dynamic kickoff, an onside kick also has to be **declared** to the officials before the kick. In 2024 it was
allowed only for a team trailing in the fourth quarter; from 2025 any time a team is trailing; and from 2026, changed
after the 2025 season, at any time at all, even when tied or ahead.[^ons26] Declaring and then booming it deep is not
an option: a declared onside kick that goes untouched past the receiving team's 15-yard onside setup zone is a
15-yard unsportsmanlike-conduct penalty, and the receiving team takes the ball.

That word "declared" changed the play completely. A surprise onside kick, the most famous trick play in the kicking
game, is now illegal: the receiving team always knows it is coming, so the hands team is always on the field. Add
the lost running start (gone since 2018), and the recovery rate collapsed. Under the dynamic kickoff, declared onside
kicks were recovered by the kicking team `{python} pct(ONS.rec[2024])` of the time in 2024 and
`{python} pct(ONS.rec[2025])` in 2025 (about 50 tries a season, so the figures are noisy).[^calcons] In October 2025
the league's head of football operations, Troy Vincent, said that "when you start getting a less than 5% recovery
rate," it may be time for the owners to "revisit" the play.[^ap2025] He was looking at the start of the 2025 season:
through Week 7, kicking teams had recovered `{python} f"{int(ONS25_EARLY.own_kickoff_recovery.sum())}"` of
`{python} f"{len(ONS25_EARLY)}"` declared onside kicks, about `{python} pct(ONS25_EARLY.own_kickoff_recovery.mean())`.
The rest of the season was kinder, which is how the full-season figure ended near one in ten.[^calcwk7] A proposed
alternative, letting a trailing team keep the ball by converting a fourth-and-long play from scrimmage instead, has
been voted down or withdrawn several times.[^eagles]

Why allow an onside kick "at any time" in 2026? It does not bring the surprise back, since it still has to be
declared. What it adds is the option for teams that are *not* trailing. The clearest case is a tie: a team kicking
off late in a tied game, or to start overtime. The overtime rules guarantee each team a chance to possess the ball,
and a kickoff counts as the receiving team's chance, so a kicking team that recovers an onside kick to open overtime
has used up the other team's guaranteed possession.[^ot] It is a long shot either way, but it now exists.

```{python}
#| label: fig-onside
#| fig-cap: "A declared onside kick, aligned as the 2026 rulebook requires. The kicking team lines up on its own 35 beside the ball, five on each side, with at least two outside the yard numbers and two between the numbers and the hashes on each side; the receiving team's restraining line is ten yards away (dotted), with nine of its players (here the hands team, orange) within 15 yards of that line. The kicker drives the ball into the ground toward one sideline (here the kicker's left, the top of the picture) so it takes a big hop past the 10-yard line, and the three kicking players on that side race to where it comes down, with a fourth trailing to scoop it if it squirts loose. The hands team's front row (H) sets a yard or two behind the restraining line to play the hop."
kick = [K_("K", -6.0, 0.0, "K")]
kick += [K_(f"C{i + 1}", -0.8, w) for i, w in enumerate([-23.5, -20.5, -14, -9, -4, 4, 9, 14, 20.5, 23.5])]
ret = [RT_(f"H{i + 1}", 13.0, w, "H") for i, w in enumerate([-19.5, -14, -9, -4, 1, 6, 11])]
ret += [RT_(f"B{i + 1}", 19.0, w) for i, w in enumerate([-12, -3])]
ret += [RT_("DR", 28.0, 4.0), RT_("KR1", R(18), 0.0, "KR")]
o = Play(kick, ret, los=KICK_X, to_go=None)
o.highlight("KR1", color=DC)
for c, end in [("C1", (10.6, -21.6)), ("C2", (10.9, -18.8)), ("C3", (10.6, -15.4)), ("C4", (8.4, -11.0))]:
    o.path(c, [end], absolute=True)
fo = fix_field(o.draw(orient="horizontal", lateral="full", window=(-11.0, 52.0), title=False, width_in=5.4))
(x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P_(fo, o, 0.0, 0.0), P_(fo, o, 11.6, -17.2)
fo.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9, color=style.BALL, lw=1.3,
                                ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=6, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.35"))
land(fo, o, 11.6, -17.2)
ball(fo, o, 0.0, 0.0)
line_across(fo, o, 10.0, style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1.5, 1.5)))
say(fo, o, 17.5, 22.0, "10 yards: the ball\nmust reach this line\nbefore the kicking\nteam may touch it",
    fontsize=6.2)
arrow(fo, o, (11.8, 22.0), (10.2, 22.0), style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ms=6)
say(fo, o, 20.0, -20.0, "the hop comes\ndown here", color=style.BALL, fontsize=6.4)
arrow(fo, o, (16.6, -19.2), (12.6, -17.6), style.BALL, lw=0.9, ms=6)
say(fo, o, 24.5, 13.0, "hands team: sure-handed\nreceivers, backs, DBs", color=DC, fontsize=6.6)
say(fo, o, -6.0, -6.5, "kicker", color=OC, fontsize=6.6)
clip_texts(fo)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"An onside kick is a desperation play that works about one time in five." It rarely worked even that often: from
2010 to 2017 kicking teams recovered roughly one onside kick in seven, and only surprise kicks did much better.[^calcons2]
Under the declared-onside rules, it works roughly one time in ten or worse, because the receiving team is never
surprised and the kicking team has no running start.
:::

## Field position, kickoff by kickoff: what it adds up to

Pull the threads together. In 2025 the average drive after a kickoff started at the
`{python} f"{BY.start[2025]:.1f}"`, against `{python} f"{BY.start[2023]:.1f}"` in 2023 (onside kicks and return
touchdowns excluded).[^calcstart] That league-wide shift helps both teams equally, since both teams receive
kickoffs; it changes how games are played (drives start closer to scoring range), not who wins them.

What decides games is the gap *between* two teams' kickoff units. Here the arithmetic is simple. A team kicks off
about `{python} f"{KO_PER_TEAM25:.0f}"` times in a season. The best kicking unit of 2025 held opponents about
`{python} f"{GAP_BEST:.1f}"` yards below the league average after its kickoffs, worth about
`{python} f"{GAP_BEST * EP_YD * KO_PER_TEAM25:.0f}"` points over the season at `{python} f"{EP_YD:.2f}"` points a
yard; the worst gave up about `{python} f"{GAP_WORST:.1f}"` yards more than average, costing about
`{python} f"{GAP_WORST * EP_YD * KO_PER_TEAM25:.0f}"`. Between the two, that is roughly
`{python} f"{(GAP_BEST + GAP_WORST) * EP_YD * KO_PER_TEAM25:.0f}"` points, several field goals, earned on a play
most viewers use to get a snack.

There is a quieter consequence too. A drive that starts at the 30 instead of the 25 is that much closer to
[field-goal range](09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd). Fourth-down and end-of-half decisions in
[Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) start from where the
drive started, and the dynamic kickoff moved that starting point up the field.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New Orleans Saints 2024"}
**What happened:** in the first season of the dynamic kickoff, many teams simply kicked into the end zone and took
the touchback at the 30. The Saints' Blake Grupe went the other way: every one of his first nine kickoffs of the season
landed at or inside the 5-yard line.[^ringer] Over the season, the Saints' opponents started their drives after
kickoffs at the `{python} f"{TEAM24.start['NO']:.1f}"` on average, the best in the league; the league average was the
`{python} f"{BY.start[2024]:.1f}"`.[^calcno]

**What to notice:** on a Saints kickoff, watch the ball, not the returner. Does it come down near the goal line,
not the 15? Does it bounce before it is fielded, so the coverage is already moving while the returner chases it?
That combination, a kick that comes down deep in the landing zone and is hard to field cleanly, was the blueprint
other teams copied once the touchback moved to the 35.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chicago Bears 2024, Week 1"}
**What happened:** in the first regular-season week of the dynamic kickoff, the Bears popped a good return against
Tennessee by having two blockers double-team one cover man and pulling another blocker across to pick off a cover man
who would otherwise have been unblocked. Analysts singled it out, and at least nine other teams used double teams on
returns that same opening week.[^bears] Under the current rulebook only setup-zone players may take part in a double
team, so a scheme like this builds its extra hat from the setup zone, not from the second returner.

**What to notice:** on any 2025 or 2026 return, look for two receiving players lined up close together across from
one cover man, or one blocker who moves sideways at the catch instead of straight ahead. That pair is the point of
attack, and the returner's lane will be beside it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New Orleans Saints, Super Bowl XLIV (2009 season)"}
**What happened:** the Saints opened the second half of Super Bowl XLIV, on February 7, 2010, with a surprise onside
kick. Thomas Morstead's short kick bounced off a Colts player and New Orleans recovered, then drove for a touchdown in
a 31-17 win.[^ambush] Sean Payton's call, known as "Ambush," is probably the most famous onside kick ever.

**What to notice:** everything that made it work is now illegal or gone. The Colts' return team was set up for a deep
kick, with no hands team on the field, because nobody expected an onside kick to open a half while a team was
trailing by only four. Under the declared-onside rule that surprise cannot happen; the officials would tell the
receiving team, and the hands team would trot on.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: the field-position ledger.** Kickoffs come in bunches (after every score and to start each half), so
there is time to read each one.

*Before the kick*

- Count the receiving team's players on its 35 and the floaters behind them. Under the 2026 rules expect five on the
  line and up to four behind. Is there a pair of floaters close together across from one cover man? That is a likely
  double team, and the return will probably go beside it.
- How many returners? Two deep usually means a standard return. One deep means ten in the setup zone, so count six on
  the 35; the team may expect a short or bouncing kick.
- Late in a half, or with a dangerous returner: expect a squib, or a kick toward a corner, away from him.

*While the ball is in the air*

- Where does it come down? End zone in the air (kneel = the 35), landing zone and roll-in (kneel = the 20), landing
  zone (field it), or short (ball at the 40).
- Did it bounce first? A bouncing ball releases the coverage while the returner is still fielding it. How deep was it
  caught? The deeper the catch, the longer the blocks must hold.

*After the play*

- Write down the starting yard line. Do it for every kickoff by both teams, and average each column at the end of the
  game.
- Compare with the league average: about the 30 in 2025. A team whose kickoffs are consistently two yards better than
  its opponent's is gaining more than half a point a game (two yards, times about
  `{python} f"{EP_YD:.2f}"` points a yard, times the five or so kickoffs each team makes), quietly.
- Did a returner run a ball out of the end zone and get stopped short of the 35? That is a mistake worth noting. Was a
  good return called back for holding? Note that too.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. Kneel or run?** The kickoff comes down at the 4, bounces once and skips into the end zone, where the
returner picks it up three yards deep. Under the 2026 rules, should he take a knee or run it out? Would your answer
change if the same kick had come down in the end zone on the fly?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: the kick comes down at the receiving team's 4 (X), inside the landing zone, and rolls into the end zone (dotted), where the returner (KR) picks it up three yards deep. The coverage was released when the ball landed and is closing. Kneel or run?"
kick = [K_(f"C{i + 1}", 33.0 + (i % 3) * 1.6, w) for i, w in enumerate(COVER_W)]
ret = [RT_(f"B{i + 1}", R(29.5), w) for i, w in enumerate([-20, -10, 0, 10, 20])]
ret += [RT_(f"F{i + 1}", R(27), w) for i, w in enumerate([-19, -3, 3, 19])]
ret += [RT_("KR1", R(-3), 1.5, "KR"), RT_("KR2", R(12), -12.0, "KR")]
d1 = Play(kick, ret, los=KICK_X, to_go=None)
d1.highlight("KR1", color=DC)
f = fix_field(d1.draw(orient="horizontal", lateral="full", window=(18.0, 75.0), title=False, width_in=5.2))
band(f, d1, R(20), R(0), style.LINE_TO_GAIN, 0.12)
line_across(f, d1, R(20), style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1.5, 1.5)))
arrow(f, d1, (41.0, 1.5), (R(4), 1.5), style.BALL, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 2)), ms=7)
land(f, d1, R(4), 1.5)
(xa, ya), (xb, yb) = P_(f, d1, R(4), 1.5), P_(f, d1, R(-2.2), 1.5)
f.ax.plot([xa, xb], [ya, yb], color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (1, 1.2)), zorder=8)
say(f, d1, R(4), -3.5, "lands at the 4", color=style.BALL, fontsize=7)
say(f, d1, R(-3), 7.5, "fielded 3 yards\ndeep", color=DC, fontsize=7)
say(f, d1, 25.5, -12.0, "coverage released\nat the landing", color=OC, fontsize=7)
clip_texts(f)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Run it out.** The kick came down in the landing zone before rolling into the end zone, so a knee gives his team the
ball only at the 20, and returns fielded in the end zone averaged about the `{python} f"{EZ25.start.mean():.0f}"` in
2025. If the same kick had landed in the end zone on the fly, the knee would be worth the 35, and he should almost
always take it: those returns reached the 35 only `{python} pct((EZ25.start >= 35).mean())` of the time. This is why
kickers love the line drive that lands at the 3 and skips in: it forces the returner either to accept the 20 or to run
out from deep in his end zone.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. Twenty-two seconds.** It's the end of the first half. You have just kicked a field goal to go up 13-10
with 0:22 left, and you are about to kick off. The other team has one timeout and a dangerous returner (KR1, the
deeper of the two). Under the 2026 rules, which of the four kicks in the picture do you want, and which must you
avoid?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: the kickoff after a field goal with 0:22 left in the first half; the kicking team leads 13-10 and the receiving team has one timeout. The kicker's four options: A, into the end zone (touchback at the 35, no time off the clock); B, deep into the landing zone; C, a squib that hits the ground around the 15, away from the dangerous returner; D, short of the 20 or out of bounds. Which one?"
kick, ret = dynamic_units()
d2 = Play(kick, ret, los=KICK_X, to_go=None)
d2.highlight("KR1", "KR2", color=DC)
f = fix_field(d2.draw(orient="horizontal", lateral="full", window=(-11.0, 75.0), title=False, width_in=5.6))
band(f, d2, R(35), R(30), style.DEFENSE, 0.10)
band(f, d2, R(20), R(0), style.LINE_TO_GAIN, 0.12)
ball(f, d2, 0.0, 0.0)
for name, (d, w), rad, dw in [("A", (R(-6), 9.0), -0.10, 2.9), ("B", (R(4), -9.0), 0.10, -2.9),
                              ("C", (R(15), -16.0), 0.12, -2.9), ("D", (R(27), 13.0), -0.12, 2.9)]:
    arrow(f, d2, (0.6, 0.0), (d, w), style.BALL, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), ms=7, rad=rad)
    land(f, d2, d, w)
    say(f, d2, d, w + dw, name, color=style.BALL, fontsize=8, weight="bold")
say(f, d2, 7.5, -18.5, "0:22 left in the half\nKicking team leads 13-10\nReceiving team: 1 timeout",
    color=style.INK, fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
say(f, d2, R(4.5), 13.0, "dangerous\nreturner", color=DC, fontsize=6.8)
clip_texts(f)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**B or C: make them field it, and never D.** A touchback (A) hands the receiving team the ball at its 35 *with all 22
seconds on the clock*, because the clock doesn't start until the ball is touched in the field of play. From the 35,
two quick sideline completions of 15 to 20 yards and a timeout can set up a long field goal. A kick that has to be
returned does two things for you. It usually ends short of the 35 (around the 28-30 on average in 2025), and the clock
runs from the moment the returner touches it, so a five- or six-second return leaves them about 16 seconds from
somewhere near their 30: time for two or three plays, if they get out of bounds or use the timeout. Against a dangerous
returner, many coaches choose C, a squib that bounces away from him, giving up a couple of yards for the near-certainty
that there is no long return. What you must avoid is D: the ball at the 40 with 22 seconds left is a gift. The clock
rules behind this are in [Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. Down eight, a minute left.** You have just scored a touchdown, but the two-point try failed, and you trail
by 8 with 1:01 left in the fourth quarter. You have no timeouts. Do you kick off deep or declare an onside kick? If you
declare it, what will the receiving team put on the field, and what are your chances?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: trailing by 8 with 1:01 left and no timeouts, the kicking team has to choose before it lines up, because the two kicks use different alignments. Left: the dynamic-kickoff alignment for a deep kick, coverage on the receiving 40. Right: a declared onside kick, coverage beside the ball and the receiving team ten yards away; told in advance, it sends out its hands team (H)."
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 5.0))
WIN3 = (-9.0, 72.0)
kick, ret = dynamic_units()
d3 = Play(kick, ret, los=KICK_X, to_go=None)
d3.highlight("KR1", "KR2", color=DC)
g1 = fix_field(d3.draw(ax=a1, lateral="full", window=WIN3, title=False))
band(g1, d3, R(35), R(30), style.DEFENSE, 0.10)
band(g1, d3, R(20), R(0), style.LINE_TO_GAIN, 0.12)
ball(g1, d3, 0.0, 0.0)
say(g1, d3, 13.0, 0.0, "coverage on\ntheir 40", color=OC, fontsize=6.6)
say(g1, d3, R(12), 0.0, "returners deep", color=DC, fontsize=6.6)
clip_texts(g1)
a1.set_title("Deep kick", fontsize=8.5, loc="left", color=style.INK)
kick = [K_("K", -6.0, 0.0, "K")]
kick += [K_(f"C{i + 1}", -0.8, w) for i, w in enumerate([-23.5, -20.5, -14, -9, -4, 4, 9, 14, 20.5, 23.5])]
ret = [RT_(f"H{i + 1}", 13.0, w, "H") for i, w in enumerate([-19.5, -14, -9, -4, 1, 6, 11])]
ret += [RT_(f"B{i + 1}", 19.0, w) for i, w in enumerate([-12, -3])]
ret += [RT_("DR", 28.0, 4.0), RT_("KR1", R(18), 0.0, "KR")]
o3 = Play(kick, ret, los=KICK_X, to_go=None)
o3.highlight("KR1", color=DC)
g2 = fix_field(o3.draw(ax=a2, lateral="full", window=WIN3, title=False))
ball(g2, o3, 0.0, 0.0)
line_across(g2, o3, 10.0, style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1.5, 1.5)))
say(g2, o3, 5.0, 0.0, "coverage beside\nthe ball", color=OC, fontsize=6.6)
say(g2, o3, 16.4, 6.5, "hands team (H)", color=DC, fontsize=6.6)
say(g2, o3, 40.0, 0.0, "nobody deep but\none returner", color=DC, fontsize=6.6)
clip_texts(g2)
a2.set_title("Declared onside kick", fontsize=8.5, loc="left", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Declare the onside kick.** If you kick deep with no timeouts, the other team takes over and kneels; each kneel keeps
the clock running and uses up to 40 seconds of play clock, so the game ends without you touching the ball again. Your
only hope is to recover the kick. The receiving team knows it is coming (the kick had to be declared), so it puts its
hands team on the field: receivers, tight ends, backs and defensive backs, players chosen for their hands rather than
their blocking. Your kicker will aim a hard, hopping kick toward one sideline so his fastest players can get to it just
past the 10-yard line. Your chances are poor: under the declared-onside rules, kicking teams recovered
`{python} pct(ONS.rec[2024])` of onside kicks in 2024 and `{python} pct(ONS.rec[2025])` in 2025. And recovering is only
step one: you would still need a touchdown and a two-point conversion in under a minute with no timeouts, so your real
chance of winning is far smaller than the recovery rate. Poor beats zero, though. With more time and timeouts (say
3:30 and three timeouts) the answer flips: kick deep, play defense, and use the timeouts to get the ball back with good
field position, because a failed onside kick hands the other team the ball near midfield. Where exactly the line falls
is a [win probability](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd) question.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- A **kickoff** is a free kick that trades field position after a score. For fifteen years the league made it safer
  by making it disappear, until only about a quarter of kickoffs were returned in 2023.
- The **dynamic kickoff** (2024) took away the distance instead: the coverage stands on the receiving team's 40, five
  yards from blockers in the **setup zone**, and nobody but the kicker and returners moves until the ball lands in the
  **landing zone**. Returns rose and kickoff concussions fell.
- The rules keep moving. **2025:** touchback to the 35, onside kicks declarable whenever trailing. **2026** (changed
  after the 2025 season): onside kicks declarable at any time, only five receivers on the restraining line with up to
  four floaters, and touchbacks on kicks from the 50 spotted at the 20.
- The **touchback math** drives everything: in 2025 a returned kick started, on average, around the 29 to 31, short of
  the 35 a touchback gives, and the deeper the kick was fielded the worse the return did, because the coverage always
  starts at the 40. So kickers aim deep into the landing zone, returners should usually kneel on a ball that lands in
  the end zone, and they should run out one that rolled in.
- A return is now a **run play**: ten blockers for eleven cover men, so the scheme leaves the kicker for the returner
  to beat and one backside cover man free, and spends the spare blocker on a **double team** (setup-zone players only)
  at the point of attack.
- **Onside kicks** must be declared, so the **hands team** is always waiting and the surprise onside is gone. Recovery
  rates fell to around one in ten or worse.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From simulation to real tracking data.** The return animation above is a gridiron simulation written in NFL Big Data
Bowl coordinates. The 2022 Big Data Bowl was about special teams and released tracking data for every kickoff, punt and
field goal from the 2018-2020 seasons, so you can draw real kickoffs with the same code. Those are traditional
kickoffs, which makes them a good contrast with the simulated dynamic kickoff here.
The data is on Kaggle and needs your own free login, so this code is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (a real kickoff from Big Data Bowl 2022 files; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2022/plays.csv")
games = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2022/games.csv")
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb2022/tracking2018.csv")   # one file per season: tracking2018/2019/2020.csv
ko = plays[(plays["specialTeamsPlayType"] == "Kickoff") & plays["gameId"].isin(trk["gameId"].unique())]
g, pl = ko.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
# In the 2022 files 'team' is home / away / football, so map it to club abbreviations for prepare()
abbr = games.set_index("gameId")[["homeTeamAbbr", "visitorTeamAbbr"]]
one = trk[(trk.gameId == g) & (trk.playId == pl)].copy()
home, away = abbr.loc[g]
one["club"] = one["club"].map({"home": home, "away": away, "football": "football"})
one = bdb.prepare(one, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)     # possessionTeam = the kicking team here
kick_frame = one.loc[one["event"] == "kickoff", "frameId"].min()
one["time"] = (one["frameId"] - kick_frame) / 10.0        # time from the kick, not from a snap
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0])
```

[^freekick]: NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 6-1-1 (free kicks; the kick after a safety may be a punt,
    dropkick or placekick from the 20) and Rule 11-4-3 (the fair-catch kick is a field-goal attempt from the spot of
    the fair catch): <https://static.www.nfl.com/image/upload/fl_attachment/league/tqivdkzt9mu6wdgsh1ku.pdf>, linked
    from <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.
[^epcurve]: Course calculation: average nflverse expected points for first-and-10 plays outside the last two minutes
    of a half, 2023-2025 regular seasons, by yard line; the per-yard figure is the slope of a straight line fitted to
    the 20 through the 40. Single five-yard steps on the raw curve bounce around it (from the 30 to the 35 is about
    0.2, from the 25 to the 30 about 0.3) because each yard line's average is an estimate; the fitted slope is the
    steadier number, and it is the one this chapter uses.

    Football Operations, "Evolution of the NFL rules": <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/evolution-of-the-nfl-rules/>.

    ball in a regular-season overtime) and Rule 16-1-5(c): "A kickoff is the opportunity to possess for the receiving
    team. If the kicking team legally recovers the kick, the receiving team is considered to have had its opportunity."
[^calcons2]: Course calculation (method as above): onside recovery rates by season, 2010-2017, ranged from about 11%
    to 21% and averaged about 15%.

    earlier in the chapter.
